description: We’re five students interested in engineering, physics, medicine, finance, law, AI and technology. We love solving problems, building things and combining different skills. For Space Apps 2026, we’re creating Mission: Vector, an interactive space mission design game.
summary: Mission: Vector is a space mission design game we built for NASA Space Apps 2026. We wanted people to experience what actually goes into planning a space mission. Players can design a spacecraft for the Moon or Mars, choose their equipment, manage their budget, and see how their decisions affect the mission. They can then run a simulation, see what went wrong, and improve their design. We've also added an asteroid minigame, mission animations, and real NASA/JPL data for orbital calculations. Our aim was simple: make space engineering fun and show that even the smallest decisions can make or break an entire mission.
details:
Mission: Vector - Project Details

What does our project do?

Mission: Vector is basically a game where you get to design your own spacecraft and see whether it would actually survive a mission to the Moon or Mars. You choose everything from the rocket and propulsion system to the power supply, communications and scientific instruments. But there's a catch. Every component affects something else. You might have the best scientific equipment, but if your spacecraft is too heavy, too expensive or doesn't have enough power, your mission isn't going anywhere. Once you're happy with your design, you can simulate the mission, see what worked, what failed and try again.

How does it work?

We used simplified engineering and physics calculations to make the game work. These include the rocket equation for propulsion, mass and fuel calculations, power consumption, communications, mission costs and the reliability of different components. The game uses these calculations to work out whether your spacecraft is capable of completing its objectives. There's also an optimization feature that lets you compare different spacecraft designs and see which trade-offs work better.

NASA Data

We used NASA/JPL reference data for Earth, the Moon and Mars, including their gravitational parameters and radii. From this, the game calculates things like orbital velocity, orbital periods, escape velocity and gravity. We also included solar irradiance calculations, NASA images and scientific facts with links to their sources. The spacecraft costs, reliability figures and some mission parameters are estimates made for the game, rather than official NASA values.

Other Features

We didn't want the entire game to just be selecting components and looking at numbers, so we added an asteroid survival minigame where you fly a spacecraft, dodge asteroids, shoot obstacles and collect science coins while trying to keep your hull intact. There's also a leaderboard, animated mission paths, an in-game assistant to help players understand what they're doing, and a science archive with NASA facts.

Technology and Development

We built the game using HTML, CSS and JavaScript, so it runs directly in a browser without needing to install anything. Our team worked on the ideas, game mechanics, design choices, testing and improvements throughout development.

What Makes It Different?

We wanted to make something that was both a game and a way to learn about space engineering. Instead of just reading about rockets or memorising equations, players get to make their own decisions and see the consequences. Sometimes a design looks perfect until you realize you've completely overlooked something important. That's exactly what makes the game interesting.

What Do We Hope to Achieve?

Our main goal is to get more people interested in space, physics and engineering without making it feel like another school lesson. We wanted to show how much thought goes into even a relatively simple space mission and how one small decision can affect everything else. If someone finishes playing with a better understanding of spacecraft design, or even just a bit more curiosity about space, then we've achieved what we set out to do.
